idiom_name: Wicked steps DSL on the controller + AASM state machine on the model
implementation_notes: Rails itself provides the front controller (routes) and page controllers (ActionController subclasses), so in Ruby the application controller comes from gems that split it in two: Wicked includes a steps DSL into one controller (include Wicked::Wizard; steps :select, :amount, :confirm) and drives the step routes so a single controller owns the sequence, while AASM puts the guarded transitions on the model (aasm do state :select; event :choose transitions ... end) and the controller asks can_choose? before advancing. What replaces the classic controller-plus-command objects is that split - the step list declares the flow, the model's state machine declares the guards - which fits Rails' convention-over-configuration style; hand-write a decision table when the flow is not a linear wizard over a persisted resource or when the steps must be data.
code_sketch:
class OrderStepsController < ApplicationController
  include Wicked::Wizard
  steps :select, :amount, :confirm          # the flow, declared once

  def update
    @order.assign_attributes(order_params)
    render_wizard @order          # advances only when the record is valid
  end
end
pitfalls: Rails' own base class is literally named ApplicationController but is a Page Controller: putting flow state or navigation rules there spreads them across every controller - the flow belongs to the step controller or the model, not to the base class.

Wicked advances the step when the record saves, so an invalid form silently keeps the user on the same step; guards that depend on more than validity (roles, branches) must be explicit before render_wizard.
Step progress kept only in the session is lost on restart or when the session store is cleared; keep the authoritative step as an AASM state on the model when the conversation must survive.
